idiom_name: context managers (@contextmanager), decorators and descriptors; Streamlit st.session_state for rerun UIs
implementation_notes: Python realizes the pattern with ordinary language constructs rather than a host runtime: contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator into a context manager whose finally block is the documented guaranteed cleanup path, decorators and descriptors package state around callables and attributes (functools.cached_property caches per instance), and closures capture per-use state without any framework participation. In UI frameworks with a rerun model the analogue is explicit: Streamlit's st.session_state shares variables between reruns per user session, widget callbacks run before the script re-executes, and caching decorators keep expensive work across reruns - so the reusable unit is a plain function reading and writing the session store instead of calling slot primitives. Prefer the context manager or a small class when cleanup matters, and keep the session-state form inside the framework because it is meaningless outside the rerun host.
pitfalls: A @contextmanager generator runs once per with statement: a single instance may not be reused, and the documented ContextDecorator behaviour only creates a fresh generator when it is used as a decorator.
Exceptions raised inside the with block are re-raised at the yield point; catching them in the except clause silently marks them handled unless they are re-raised.
Streamlit reruns the whole script on every interaction, so state kept in ordinary locals is lost - only st.session_state, caching or another external store survives a rerun.
